verses.1: Al-Mizan takes the address as a censure concerning the Prophet’s personal life, signalled by ‘Prophet’ rather than ‘Messenger,’ not his mission. He had sworn a yamīn to refrain from something God had made lawful in order to please wives who had troubled him over it. This taḥrīm is self-forbidding through an oath, not legislation making a lawful thing unlawful in the sharīʿah, which would not be his place. Although the wording censures him, the later command to the two wives to repent and the description of God as Forgiving and Merciful show that the censure is fundamentally directed at them.
verses.2: Al-Mizan preserves al-Rāghib’s distinction: faraḍa Allāh ʿalā denotes an obligation upon all Muslims, including the Prophet, while faraḍa Allāhu li- indicates that he may not bar himself from the act at issue. Taḥillah means dissolving an oath through kaffārah, the means God has made clear for undoing its binding. The verse thus permits the nullification of oaths through expiation and commands the Prophet to rescind the oath he had made. God is the walī who manages believers’ affairs through wise, knowing legislation and guidance.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains sirr as a private secret and isrār as entrusting it to someone while requiring secrecy. It identifies the wife as Ḥafṣah bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: the Prophet confided a secret to her, she disclosed it to another against his wish, and God informed him of that disclosure. He told her of part of what had occurred and withheld the rest; when she asked who had told him, he answered that the Knowing, Aware One had informed him. The account displays God’s knowledge of both what is hidden and what is manifest.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says the two addressed are ʿĀʾishah and Ḥafṣah, as narrations concur. Their ṣaghw is an inclination to falsehood away from rectitude, and by vexing and uniting against the Prophet they committed a major sin. The plural ‘hearts’ conventionally denotes their two hearts, while taẓāhur means mutual support against him. God’s being his mawlā signals His direct, special care for the Prophet, while Gabriel, the righteous among the believers, and the angels stand as his supporters. Though the wording can grammatically suggest the collective righteous, Sunni reports from the Prophet and Shiʿi reports from the Imams identify the righteous one as ʿAlī; other views are unsupported. The singular aide depicts the angels’ unified support. The surrounding shifts of address and partial concealment of the event are read as divine support for the Prophet, placing the wives before repentance or the knowledge of this support and then unfolding the chapter’s contrasts between faithlessness and faith.
verses.5: Al-Mizan sees the threatened replacement as demonstrating God’s self-sufficiency: marriage to the Prophet does not itself confer nobility before God, which rests on piety. The listed qualities—submission, faith, devout obedience, repentance, worship, fasting, and being virgins or previously married—make such wives genuinely better. Their superiority chiefly rests on qunūt and repentance, or perhaps qunūt alone, since it is the humility prerequisite to obedience; Mary’s later description supports this. The commentary rejects the view that ‘better’ merely contrasts the present wives with women the Prophet had formerly divorced, since then all present wives would share the decisive distinction and the enumerated virtues would be pointless. Al-Kashshāf explains why the qualities are unconnected except for virgin and otherwise: those two are opposites and cannot coexist in one person.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains qū as safeguarding and waqūd as the material that kindles a fire. The fire is hell, its punished people are themselves its fuel, and stones may mean idols; this and the following verse support the embodiment of deeds in the hereafter. Its stern, strong angels administer punishment: their harsh office explains ghilāẓ, and shidād denotes strength in resolve and action. Their not disobeying describes strict adherence to their charge, while doing what they are commanded describes its exact, unceasing execution; the clauses are not redundant. The view that angels will receive freely violable responsibilities in the hereafter is rejected, since they are absolutely obedient, pure beings of light who will only what God wills and are bound creationally rather than legislatively, without human-like reward and punishment. The general address calls believers to discipline themselves and their families against the fire of their clinging misdeeds.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads the address as speaking to the faithless collectively after they have entered the Fire. Their offered excuses cannot change reality: their punishment is their own deeds now laid bare and inseparably attached to them. Some exegetes instead understand the forbidden excuses as repentance offered after entering the Fire, when repentance cannot be accepted. In this context, the warning suggests that disobeying God and His Messenger may amount to kufr.
verses.8: Al-Mizan defines tawbatan naṣūḥan as repentance that permanently turns a person from the sin, so that he never returns to it. After commanding believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire, the verse gives hope that such repentance will cover misdeeds and admit them to the Garden. On that day God will not abase the Prophet or those who believed with him, hence adhered to and obeyed him; a good alternative reading makes their never separating from him in this world or at resurrection the point. Their light may be the light of faith before them and the light of their deeds on their right. Its gaps vary inversely with faith and in proportion to sins that left places unfilled in the record of servitude. Their plea for forgiveness therefore perfects the light, or is its precondition.
verses.9: Al-Mizan defines jihād as exertion to reform and to defend against harm. Against unbelievers it means proclaiming the truth, followed by fighting if they do not believe; against hypocrites it means seeking to reconcile and settle their hearts upon faith, since the Prophet did not wage war on them. It rejects the claim that severity here merely means enforcing ḥudūd on hypocrites.
verses.10: Al-Mizan notes that khiyānah originally concerned breaking pacts and trusts, while nifāq concerned religious hypocrisy, though the terms came to overlap; khiyānah is secret opposition to truth and another’s right, the opposite of amānah. The example of Noah’s and Lot’s wives shows that marriage to righteous servants brings no benefit before God when they betray. Whether ‘to those who disbelieve’ qualifies the example or its presentation, it warns disbelievers that connection to the righteous cannot save them and that betrayal of the Prophet leads to the Fire. ‘Under’ means married to, and the two prophets could not benefit their wives. Entering with those who enter may mean with their kin, as the cited histories imply, or with the faithless. The passive qīla and unconditional command convey that they have no honour before God and that their manner of perishing is of no concern.
verses.11: Al-Mizan presents Pharaoh’s wife as the believing counterpart to the preceding faithless example. Her prayer summarizes a lifetime of worship in which inward faith, outward action, heart, and speech agreed. She chose nearness to God and a house He would build for her over Pharaoh’s companionship, palace, and worldly ornaments, remaining faithful to the unseen until death and striving to remove every distraction from her Lord. Narrations name her Āsiyah. Her request joins the intangible maʿnawiyyah honour of being with her Lord to the tangible ṣūriyyah honour of dwelling in the Garden. By asking rescue from Pharaoh and his deeds, she dissociates herself from wrongdoing she might be thought to share as his companion; some exegetes take his ‘doing’ to mean the conjugal act. Her further request for rescue from the unjust people separates her from Pharaoh’s whole society, not only his household and court.
verses.12: Al-Mizan presents Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, as a further example for believers and notes that God alone among women is praised by name in the Qur’an. Her guarded chastity is repeatedly praised and may answer the Jews’ calumny against her. The commentary accepts that her affirming her Lord’s words means belief in revelation to the prophets, rejecting the explanation that it means heaven, hell, commands, and prohibitions because that would already include the books. Those books include revealed laws such as the Torah, Gospel, and Qur’an; her acceptance of the words may also indicate that she was ṣiddīqah. ‘The obedient ones’ means all who humbly and loyally obey God, supported by qunūt in the address to Mary, rather than her particular righteous clan; the latter reading is unlikely, especially given the example’s address to the Prophet’s wives.
